content: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is one of the most prevalent human viruses globally. It is primarily transmitted through bodily fluids, with saliva being the main route of spread. EBV is also referred to as human herpesvirus 4 and belongs to the herpesvirus family. Most individuals will encounter EBV at some point in their lives, often during childhood. Infections in children are typically asymptomatic or present with symptoms that are indistinguishable from other mild, short-lived childhood illnesses. EBV is the leading cause of infectious mononucleosis, commonly known as mono. This contagious illness is frequently observed in teenagers and adults. The symptoms of EBV infection can include fatigue, fever, an inflamed throat, swollen lymph nodes in the neck, an enlarged spleen, a swollen liver, and a rash. While most individuals who develop symptoms recover within 2 to 4 weeks, some may experience prolonged fatigue lasting several weeks or even months. Once a person is infected with EBV, the virus remains latent (inactive) in their body. In certain cases, the virus can reactivate, though this does not always result in symptoms. However, individuals with weakened immune systems are more likely to exhibit symptoms if the virus reactivates. EBV is highly contagious during the initial infection phase and can be spread for weeks, even before symptoms appear. Once the virus establishes itself in the body, it remains dormant but can reactivate at any time, potentially allowing the infected individual to transmit the virus to others, regardless of how much time has passed since the initial infection. The virus is most commonly spread through saliva, which can occur via kissing, sharing drinks or food, using the same drinking cups, eating utensils, or toothbrushes, or coming into contact with toys that have been drooled on by children. EBV can also be transmitted through blood and semen during sexual contact, blood transfusions, and organ transplants. The virus is thought to survive on objects as long as the surface remains moist. Currently, there is no vaccine available to prevent EBV infection. To reduce the risk of infection, it is advisable to avoid close contact with individuals who have an active EBV infection. Specifically, you should refrain from kissing, sharing drinks or food, and using personal items that an infected person has recently used. Diagnosing EBV infection can be challenging because its symptoms overlap with those of other illnesses. A blood test that detects antibodies specific to EBV can confirm the infection. Approximately 90% of adults have antibodies indicating either a current or past EBV infection. There is no specific antiviral treatment for EBV. However, supportive care can help alleviate symptoms. This includes staying hydrated by drinking plenty of fluids, getting adequate rest, and using over-the-counter medications to manage pain and fever. Most individuals recover within 2 to 4 weeks.
